name: Plato
description: Ancient Greek philosopher who founded the Academy in Athens. Developed the Theory of Forms (or Ideas), arguing that the material world is a shadow of an eternal realm of perfect Forms. His dialogues established the foundation for Western philosophy and idealist metaphysics.

name: Aristotle
description: Student of Plato who founded the Lyceum. Developed empirical approach to knowledge and formal logic. His works covered physics, metaphysics, ethics, politics, and biology. Emphasized observation and categorization as paths to understanding reality.

name: Classical Philosophy
description: Ancient Greek and Roman philosophical traditions that established fundamental questions about reality, knowledge, ethics, and politics. Emphasized rational inquiry and systematic thinking. Foundational for Western intellectual tradition.

name: Stoicism
description: Hellenistic philosophy founded by Zeno of Citium. Emphasized virtue ethics, acceptance of fate, and living in accordance with nature and reason. Taught that external events cannot harm us; only our judgments about them can. Influenced Roman thought through Seneca and Marcus Aurelius.

name: Augustine of Hippo
description: Early Christian theologian and philosopher who synthesized classical philosophy with Christian doctrine. In 'City of God' (413-426 CE), he developed a Christian philosophy of history interpreting events through divine providence, establishing the concept of linear historical time versus cyclical classical views.

name: Early Christian Thought
description: Patristic theology that integrated Greek philosophy with Christian revelation. Established theological foundations and interpretive frameworks that dominated medieval thought. Introduced linear conception of history with eschatological purpose.

name: Ibn Khaldun
description: Arab scholar who wrote the Muqaddimah (1377), developing a cyclical theory of civilizations. Pioneered sociological analysis by examining social cohesion ('asabiyyah) and economic factors in the rise and fall of dynasties. Considered a founder of sociology and historiography.

name: Islamic Philosophy
description: Medieval Islamic intellectual tradition that preserved and advanced Greek philosophy. Made major contributions to logic, metaphysics, medicine, and mathematics. Created dialogue between Aristotelian rationalism and Islamic theology.

name: Averroes
description: Ibn Rushd, Andalusian philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle. Defended rational philosophy against theological attacks. His work influenced both Islamic and Christian scholasticism, particularly Thomas Aquinas.

name: Avicenna
description: Ibn Sina, Persian polymath who synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Islamic thought. Made groundbreaking contributions to medicine and metaphysics. His 'Canon of Medicine' remained a standard medical text for centuries.
key_works: The Canon of Medicine, The Book of Healing

name: Thomas Aquinas
description: Dominican friar who synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology in his Summa Theologica (1265-1274). Developed natural law theory and five proofs for God's existence. Became the most influential medieval scholastic philosopher.

name: Scholasticism
description: Medieval philosophical tradition that used Aristotelian logic to explore theological questions. Emphasized dialectical reasoning and systematic argumentation. Dominated European universities and established methods for rational inquiry within faith.

name: Renaissance Humanism
description: Cultural and intellectual movement that revived classical learning and emphasized human dignity and agency. Developed philology and textual criticism. Challenged medieval scholasticism with focus on original sources and human experience rather than theological authority.

name: Niccolò Machiavelli
description: Florentine political philosopher who wrote 'The Prince' (1513) and 'Discourses on Livy' (1531). Pioneered political realism by analyzing power dynamics separate from moral considerations. Used historical examples to derive practical lessons about statecraft and leadership.

name: Jean Mabillon
description: Benedictine monk who published 'De re diplomatica' (1681), establishing paleography as a science for authenticating historical documents. Revolutionized historical research by providing systematic methods for source criticism and document verification.

name: Francis Bacon
description: English philosopher and statesman who developed the inductive method in 'Novum Organum' (1620). Advocated empirical observation and experimentation. Challenged Aristotelian deductive logic and proposed systematic approach to scientific inquiry.

name: Scientific Revolution
description: Period of dramatic advances in mathematics, physics, astronomy, and biology. Established experimental method and mathematical analysis of nature. Transformed understanding of cosmos from geocentric to heliocentric, laying foundations for modern science.

name: René Descartes
description: French philosopher who developed rationalist philosophy and methodological doubt. His 'Discourse on Method' (1637) established 'Cogito, ergo sum' (I think, therefore I am) as foundation for certain knowledge. Pioneered analytic geometry and mind-body dualism.
key_works: Discourse on Method, Meditations on First Philosophy

name: Isaac Newton
description: English mathematician and physicist who formulated laws of motion and universal gravitation in 'Principia Mathematica' (1687). Developed calculus and demonstrated that natural phenomena follow mathematical laws. Epitomized Scientific Revolution's synthesis of mathematics and empirical observation.

name: Rationalism
description: Philosophical tradition emphasizing reason as primary source of knowledge. Argued that certain truths can be known independently of sensory experience through innate ideas or logical deduction. Contrasted with empiricism.

name: Baruch Spinoza
description: Dutch philosopher who developed monistic metaphysics in 'Ethics' (1677). Argued for deterministic universe governed by natural laws. Identified God with Nature. Influenced later pantheism and contributed to Enlightenment secularization of philosophy.

name: Gottfried Leibniz
description: German polymath who developed monadology, calculus, and philosophical optimism. Argued for pre-established harmony and principle of sufficient reason. Contributed to logic, mathematics, and metaphysics. Envisioned universal logical language.

name: John Locke
description: English empiricist who argued in 'Essay Concerning Human Understanding' (1689) that mind begins as blank slate (tabula rasa) filled by experience. Influenced political liberalism with social contract theory. Established empiricist epistemology opposing innate ideas.
key_works: Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Two Treatises of Government

name: British Empiricism
description: Philosophical tradition asserting that knowledge comes primarily from sensory experience. Opposed Continental rationalism's emphasis on innate ideas. Established experience and observation as foundations of knowledge.

name: David Hume
description: Scottish philosopher who developed radical empiricism and skepticism in 'Treatise of Human Nature' (1739). Questioned causality, induction, and rational basis for belief. Argued that reason is slave of passions. Profoundly influenced later philosophy.
key_works: A Treatise of Human Nature, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding

name: George Berkeley
description: Irish philosopher who developed subjective idealism, arguing that material objects exist only as ideas perceived by minds. Famous dictum: 'esse est percipi' (to be is to be perceived). Challenged materialist metaphysics.
key_works: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge

name: Immanuel Kant
description: German philosopher who synthesized rationalism and empiricism in 'Critique of Pure Reason' (1781). Developed transcendental idealism and categorical imperative. Argued that mind actively structures experience through a priori categories. Revolutionary in epistemology and ethics.
key_works: Critique of Pure Reason, Critique of Practical Reason, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals

name: Enlightenment
description: Intellectual movement emphasizing reason, individual rights, scientific method, and progress. Challenged traditional authority of church and monarchy. Produced revolutions in philosophy, politics, science, and society. Established foundations for modern liberal democracy.

name: Edward Gibbon
description: English historian who wrote 'The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire' (1776-1789). Applied Enlightenment skepticism to history, analyzing religious and political factors in Rome's collapse. Established literary historical style combining narrative with critical analysis.
key_works: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

name: Voltaire
description: French Enlightenment writer and historian who pioneered cultural and social history. Advocated religious tolerance and criticized church authority. Used history to promote Enlightenment values of reason and progress.
key_works: Essay on the Customs and the Spirit of the Nations

name: Montesquieu
description: French political philosopher who wrote 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748), analyzing how laws relate to government types and social conditions. Pioneered comparative political analysis and influenced constitutional theory with separation of powers doctrine.

name: G.W.F. Hegel
description: German idealist philosopher who developed dialectical method and philosophy of history. In 'Phenomenology of Spirit' (1807) and 'Philosophy of History' (1837), argued that history progresses through dialectical process (thesis-antithesis-synthesis) toward greater freedom and self-consciousness. Profoundly influenced Marx, existentialism, and continental philosophy.
key_works: Phenomenology of Spirit, Philosophy of History, Science of Logic

name: German Idealism
description: Philosophical movement following Kant that emphasized role of mind in constituting reality. Explored consciousness, self, and absolute. Influenced by Kant's transcendental idealism but sought to overcome his thing-in-itself.

name: Johann Fichte
description: German idealist who developed subjective idealism emphasizing the self (Ich) as foundation of knowledge. Influenced early Romantic nationalism. Extended Kant's philosophy by eliminating thing-in-itself.

name: Friedrich Schelling
description: German idealist who developed philosophy of nature attempting to reconcile idealism and naturalism. Bridged Fichte and Hegel. Explored relationship between consciousness and nature through Absolute.

name: Auguste Comte
description: French philosopher who founded positivism in 'Course in Positive Philosophy' (1830-1842). Developed law of three stages (theological, metaphysical, positive) describing humanity's intellectual evolution. Coined term 'sociology' and advocated applying scientific method to study of society.
key_works: Course in Positive Philosophy, System of Positive Polity

name: Positivism
description: Philosophical approach asserting that authentic knowledge comes from sensory experience interpreted through reason and logic. Rejected metaphysics and theology as meaningless. Advocated scientific method as sole path to truth. Influenced social sciences and logical positivism.

name: Karl Marx
description: German philosopher and economist who developed historical materialism and critique of capitalism. With Engels, wrote 'Communist Manifesto' (1848) and 'Capital' (1867). Argued that economic base determines social superstructure and that history progresses through class struggle. Foundational for socialism and critical theory.
key_works: Capital, The German Ideology, Communist Manifesto (with Engels)

name: Friedrich Engels
description: German philosopher and Marx's collaborator. Co-wrote 'Communist Manifesto' (1848) and edited later volumes of 'Capital'. Applied dialectical materialism to natural sciences. Supported Marx financially and intellectually throughout their partnership.
key_works: The Communist Manifesto (with Marx), The Condition of the Working Class in England

name: Marxism
description: Revolutionary theory analyzing history through class struggle and economic relations. Argues that material conditions (base) determine social relations and ideas (superstructure). Predicts capitalism's overthrow by working class. Profoundly influenced labor movements, historiography, and critical theory.

name: Historical Materialism
description: Marxist methodology viewing history as driven by material economic conditions rather than ideas. Analyzes societies through base (economic structure) and superstructure (culture, politics, ideology). Emphasizes class relations and modes of production.

name: György Lukács
description: Hungarian Marxist philosopher who wrote 'History and Class Consciousness' (1923), developing concept of reification. Analyzed how commodity fetishism obscures social relations under capitalism. Founded Western Marxism by integrating Hegelian dialectics with Marx's materialism.
key_works: History and Class Consciousness, The Theory of the Novel

name: Frankfurt School
description: Critical theory tradition founded at Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt. Combined Marxism with psychoanalysis, sociology, and cultural criticism. Critiqued both capitalism and Soviet communism. Analyzed culture industry, instrumental reason, and domination.

name: Max Horkheimer
description: German philosopher and Frankfurt School director. Co-wrote 'Dialectic of Enlightenment' (1947) with Adorno, analyzing how Enlightenment reason becomes instrumental domination. Developed critical theory as reflexive social criticism distinguishing facts from values.
key_works: Dialectic of Enlightenment (with Adorno), Eclipse of Reason

name: Theodor Adorno
description: German philosopher, sociologist, and musicologist. Co-wrote 'Dialectic of Enlightenment' (1947) examining Enlightenment's self-destruction. Developed negative dialectics and critique of culture industry. Analyzed art's critical potential under capitalism.
key_works: Dialectic of Enlightenment (with Horkheimer), Negative Dialectics, Aesthetic Theory

name: Herbert Marcuse
description: German-American philosopher who wrote 'One-Dimensional Man' (1964), critiquing advanced industrial society's absorption of opposition. Influenced 1960s New Left. Explored liberation through aesthetics and Eros. Analyzed repressive tolerance and technological rationality.

name: Antonio Gramsci
description: Italian Marxist who developed concepts of cultural hegemony and organic intellectuals in 'Prison Notebooks' (1929-1935). Analyzed how ruling class maintains power through consent and culture, not just coercion. Influenced cultural studies and postcolonial theory.

name: Louis Althusser
description: French Marxist philosopher who argued in 'Reading Capital' (1965) for structural Marxism. Developed concept of ideological state apparatuses explaining how ideology reproduces capitalist relations. Distinguished science from ideology in Marx's work.

name: Jürgen Habermas
description: German philosopher and sociologist who developed theory of communicative action (1981). Defended rational Enlightenment project against postmodern critique. Analyzed public sphere's role in democracy. Second-generation Frankfurt School theorist.
key_works: The Theory of Communicative Action, The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere

name: E.P. Thompson
description: British Marxist historian who wrote 'The Making of the English Working Class' (1963), pioneering social history from below. Emphasized human agency and culture against economic determinism. Founded history workshop movement.
key_works: The Making of the English Working Class, The Poverty of Theory

name: Eric Hobsbawm
description: British Marxist historian who wrote monumental studies of 19th and 20th centuries. Analyzed capitalism's global spread and working-class formation. Combined economic analysis with cultural history. Influential in shaping Marxist historiography.
key_works: The Age of Revolution, The Age of Capital, The Age of Empire, The Age of Extremes

name: Leopold von Ranke
description: German historian who founded scientific history based on archival sources and source criticism. Famous for 'wie es eigentlich gewesen' (how it actually was), emphasizing objective reconstruction of past. Established seminar method and professional historical methodology in 'History of Latin and Germanic Nations' (1824).
key_works: History of the Latin and Germanic Nations, History of the Popes

name: Scientific History
description: Historical approach emphasizing objectivity, archival research, and source criticism. Sought to establish history as rigorous discipline like natural sciences. Dominated 19th-century historiography through emphasis on documents and facts.

name: Lord Acton
description: British historian who directed Cambridge Modern History project, creating collaborative encyclopedic history. Famous dictum: 'Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.' Advocated liberal Catholic historiography combining moral judgment with archival research.

name: Jacob Burckhardt
description: Swiss cultural historian who wrote 'The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy' (1860), pioneering cultural history. Emphasized art, mentality, and social customs over political events. Influenced Geistesgeschichte (history of ideas) and Annales School.
key_works: The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy, The Age of Constantine the Great

name: Annales School
description: Revolutionary French historiographical movement emphasizing long-term social and economic structures (longue durée) over political events. Founded by Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre in 1929 journal. Applied interdisciplinary methods including geography, economics, and anthropology to history.

name: Marc Bloch
description: French historian and Annales co-founder who pioneered comparative method in 'Feudal Society' (1939-1940). Integrated economic, social, and mental structures. Killed by Nazis for Resistance activities. Advocated problem-oriented history over narrative.
key_works: Feudal Society, The Royal Touch, The Historian's Craft

name: Lucien Febvre
description: French historian and Annales co-founder who developed history of mentalities. Emphasized collective psychology and mental tools (outillage mental). Advocated interdisciplinary approaches. Founded journal Annales d'histoire économique et sociale (1929) with Bloch.
key_works: The Problem of Unbelief in the Sixteenth Century, The Coming of the Book

name: Fernand Braudel
description: French historian who dominated second-generation Annales School. Developed concept of longue durée in 'The Mediterranean' (1949), distinguishing three temporal scales: geographic time (centuries), social time (decades), and individual time (events). Pioneered total history (histoire totale) integrating geography, economics, and culture.
key_works: The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II, Civilization and Capitalism

name: Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie
description: French historian of third-generation Annales School who wrote 'Montaillou' (1975), pioneering microhistory through detailed reconstruction of medieval village. Combined quantitative methods with anthropological approaches. Studied climate history and serial history.

name: Jacques Le Goff
description: French medievalist and third-generation Annales historian. Studied historical anthropology of medieval mentalities, including time, death, and purgatory. Bridged Annales structuralism with narrative history.

name: E.H. Carr
description: British historian who wrote 'What Is History?' (1961), arguing that history is dialogue between historian and facts. Challenged both empiricist objectivity and complete relativism. Established critical realism balancing evidence and interpretation. Influenced reflexive historiography.
key_works: What Is History?, A History of Soviet Russia

name: Critical Realism
description: Philosophical approach asserting that reality exists independently but knowledge is mediated by social context. In historiography, balances empiricism and constructivism. Emphasizes reflexivity about historians' biases while maintaining commitment to evidence.

name: Roy Bhaskar
description: British philosopher who developed critical realism in 'A Realist Theory of Science' (1975). Argued for stratified ontology distinguishing real, actual, and empirical domains. Applied retroductive method to social sciences. Influenced by Marx and transcendental arguments.
key_works: A Realist Theory of Science, The Possibility of Naturalism

name: Ferdinand de Saussure
description: Swiss linguist whose 'Course in General Linguistics' (1916, posthumous) founded structural linguistics. Distinguished langue (language system) from parole (individual speech), signifier from signified. Established synchronic analysis. Foundational for structuralism across disciplines.

name: Structuralism
description: Intellectual movement analyzing cultural phenomena as systems of related elements. Emphasized underlying structures over surface meanings. Applied linguistic models to anthropology, literature, and psychoanalysis. Influenced by Saussure's linguistics.

name: Claude Lévi-Strauss
description: French anthropologist who applied structural linguistics to anthropology in 'Structural Anthropology' (1958). Analyzed kinship systems, myths, and totems through binary oppositions. Argued that human mind universally structures experience through similar patterns.
key_works: Structural Anthropology, The Savage Mind, The Raw and the Cooked

name: Roland Barthes
description: French literary theorist who developed structuralist and post-structuralist semiotics. 'Mythologies' (1957) analyzed cultural signs and ideologies. 'S/Z' (1970) pioneered textual analysis. Later work emphasized pleasure of text and death of author.
key_works: Mythologies, S/Z, The Death of the Author

name: Roman Jakobson
description: Russian-American linguist who developed structural linguistics and communication theory. Identified six functions of language. Pioneered phonology. Influenced poetics through structural analysis of literary language.

name: Post-Structuralism
description: Intellectual movement challenging structuralism's claims about stable structures and binary oppositions. Emphasized instability of meaning, power/knowledge relations, and deconstruction. Influenced by Nietzsche, Freud, and Heidegger.

name: Michel Foucault
description: French philosopher who analyzed relationships between power, knowledge, and discourse. 'Madness and Civilization' (1961), 'The Order of Things' (1966), 'Discipline and Punish' (1975), and 'History of Sexuality' (1976) examined how institutions produce subjects through discourse. Developed genealogical method tracing discontinuities in history. Influenced historiography, critical theory, and social sciences.
key_works: Madness and Civilization, The Order of Things, Discipline and Punish, The History of Sexuality

name: Jacques Derrida
description: French-Algerian philosopher who developed deconstruction in 'Of Grammatology' (1967) and 'Writing and Difference' (1967). Challenged Western metaphysics' logocentrism and binary oppositions. Coined différance to indicate deferred and differing meaning. Influenced literary theory, law, and architecture.
key_works: Of Grammatology, Writing and Difference, Margins of Philosophy

name: Gilles Deleuze
description: French philosopher who developed concepts of difference, becoming, and assemblage. 'Difference and Repetition' (1968) challenged identity logic. With Guattari, wrote 'Anti-Oedipus' (1972) critiquing psychoanalysis and capitalism. Developed rhizome theory opposing hierarchical thought.
key_works: Difference and Repetition, Anti-Oedipus (with Guattari), A Thousand Plateaus (with Guattari)

name: Félix Guattari
description: French psychoanalyst and philosopher who collaborated with Deleuze on 'Anti-Oedipus' (1972) and 'A Thousand Plateaus' (1980). Developed schizoanalysis as alternative to psychoanalysis. Emphasized machinic assemblages and ecosophy.
key_works: Anti-Oedipus (with Deleuze), A Thousand Plateaus (with Deleuze), The Three Ecologies

name: Julia Kristeva
description: Bulgarian-French philosopher and psychoanalyst who developed concepts of intertextuality, abjection, and semiotic/symbolic. Integrated linguistics, psychoanalysis, and feminism. Analyzed maternal body and pre-linguistic semiotic.
key_works: Revolution in Poetic Language, Powers of Horror

name: Jean Baudrillard
description: French sociologist and philosopher who analyzed consumer society and hyperreality. 'Simulacra and Simulation' (1981) argued that signs no longer represent reality but constitute it. Developed concepts of simulation and precession of simulacra.

name: Hayden White
description: American historian who revolutionized historiography with 'Metahistory' (1973). Analyzed how historians use literary tropes (metaphor, metonymy, synecdoche, irony) to construct narratives. Argued history is as much literary as scientific, undermining claims to objective truth. Influenced postmodern historiography.
key_works: Metahistory, The Content of the Form

name: Postmodern Historiography
description: Historical approach emphasizing language, narrative, and discourse in constructing historical knowledge. Challenged objective truth claims and linear narratives. Analyzed how rhetoric and power shape historical representation. Influenced by post-structuralism and linguistic turn.

name: Dominick LaCapra
description: American intellectual historian who developed trauma theory in historiography. Analyzed how traumatic events like Holocaust challenge traditional historical representation. Emphasized working through versus acting out trauma. Integrated psychoanalysis with history.

name: Frank Ankersmit
description: Dutch philosopher of history who developed narrative substance theory. Argued that historical narratives create irreducible representations not reducible to individual statements. Emphasized aesthetics and experience in historical understanding.

name: Simone de Beauvoir
description: French existentialist philosopher and feminist theorist who wrote 'The Second Sex' (1949), foundational for modern feminism. Analyzed woman as Other constructed through patriarchal society. Famous claim: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' Developed existential feminism combining phenomenology with social critique.
key_works: The Second Sex, The Ethics of Ambiguity

name: Second Wave Feminism
description: Feminist movement focusing on sexuality, family, workplace, reproductive rights, and legal inequalities. Challenged patriarchal structures in personal and political spheres. Produced diverse theories: liberal, radical, socialist, and cultural feminism.

name: Feminist Theory
description: Intellectual tradition analyzing gender inequality and patriarchy. Emphasizes women's experiences and standpoint epistemology. Produced diverse approaches including liberal, radical, Marxist, psychoanalytic, postmodern, and intersectional feminisms.

name: Joan Wallach Scott
description: American historian who wrote 'Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis' (1986), establishing gender as central analytical framework. Integrated post-structuralist theory with women's history. Argued gender is socially constructed system of meaning structuring power relations. Pioneered feminist historiography.
key_works: Gender and the Politics of History, Only Paradoxes to Offer

name: Betty Friedan
description: American feminist activist who wrote 'The Feminine Mystique' (1963), analyzing housewife dissatisfaction and sparking second-wave feminism. Founded National Organization for Women (NOW). Advocated liberal feminism emphasizing equal opportunities.

name: Kate Millett
description: American feminist who wrote 'Sexual Politics' (1970), pioneering analysis of patriarchy in literature and theory. Coined term 'sexual politics' analyzing power in gender relations. Influenced radical feminism.

name: Germaine Greer
description: Australian feminist who wrote 'The Female Eunuch' (1970), analyzing women's oppression through family, sexuality, and capitalism. Advocated sexual liberation and revolutionary feminism.

name: bell hooks
description: American feminist theorist who wrote 'Ain't I a Woman' (1981) and 'Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center' (1984). Pioneered intersectional analysis of race, class, and gender. Critiqued mainstream feminism's exclusion of black women. Emphasized love, spirituality, and engaged pedagogy.
key_works: Ain't I a Woman, Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center, Teaching to Transgress

name: Black Feminist Thought
description: Intellectual tradition centering black women's experiences and standpoint. Analyzes interlocking oppressions of race, class, and gender. Challenges both racist exclusions in feminism and sexist exclusions in black liberation movements. Developed intersectionality as analytical framework.

name: Patricia Hill Collins
description: American sociologist who systematized black feminist thought in 'Black Feminist Thought' (1990). Developed matrix of domination analyzing intersecting systems of oppression. Identified controlling images stereotyping black women. Emphasized standpoint theory and outsider-within perspective.
key_works: Black Feminist Thought, Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory

name: Donna Haraway
description: American biologist and feminist science studies scholar who wrote 'A Cyborg Manifesto' (1985) and 'Situated Knowledges' (1988). Challenged nature/culture binary and criticized objectivity. Developed cyborg feminism and companion species theory. Later work emphasizes staying with trouble in Anthropocene.
key_works: A Cyborg Manifesto, Situated Knowledges, Staying with the Trouble, The Companion Species Manifesto

name: Judith Butler
description: American philosopher who revolutionized gender theory with 'Gender Trouble' (1990). Developed performativity theory arguing gender is enacted through repeated performances, not natural essence. Challenged sex/gender distinction and heteronormative matrix. Founded queer theory alongside feminist theory.
key_works: Gender Trouble, Bodies That Matter, Precarious Life

name: Kimberlé Crenshaw
description: American legal scholar who coined 'intersectionality' (1989) to analyze how race, class, and gender intersect in black women's experiences. Developed critical race feminism. Showed how anti-discrimination law fails to address multiple marginalization.
key_works: Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex, Mapping the Margins

name: Audre Lorde
description: American writer and activist who analyzed interconnections of racism, sexism, and homophobia. 'Sister Outsider' (1984) emphasized difference as strength and developed erotic as power. Coined 'the master's tools will never dismantle the master's house.'
key_works: Sister Outsider, The Cancer Journals, Zami: A New Spelling of My Name

name: Queer Theory
description: Intellectual tradition analyzing sexuality, gender identity, and heteronormativity. Challenges fixed categories and binary thinking about gender/sexuality. Draws on post-structuralism, feminism, and gay/lesbian studies. Emphasizes performativity and fluidity.

name: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick
description: American queer theorist who wrote 'Epistemology of the Closet' (1990), analyzing closet as fundamental structure of modern sexuality. Developed queer reading practices and affect theory. Challenged homo/heterosexual binary.
key_works: Epistemology of the Closet, Touching Feeling

name: Jack Halberstam
description: American queer theorist who wrote 'Female Masculinity' (1998), analyzing masculinity detached from male bodies. Developed concepts of queer time and queer failure. Studies transgender issues and alternative kinship.
key_works: Female Masculinity, The Queer Art of Failure, Trans*

name: Science and Technology Studies
description: Interdisciplinary field studying how social, political, and cultural factors shape science and technology, and vice versa. Challenges science's objectivity claims. Emphasizes situated knowledge and material practices. Key approaches include social construction of technology (SCOT) and actor-network theory (ANT).

name: Bruno Latour
description: French philosopher and anthropologist who developed actor-network theory (ANT). 'Laboratory Life' (1979) pioneered laboratory studies. 'We Have Never Been Modern' (1991) challenged nature/culture divide. Emphasized symmetry between human and non-human actors. Applied ANT to ecology and politics.
key_works: Laboratory Life, Science in Action, We Have Never Been Modern, Reassembling the Social

name: Michel Callon
description: French sociologist who developed translation theory within actor-network theory. Analyzed how heterogeneous actors are enrolled and aligned. Studied techno-economic networks.
key_works: Some Elements of a Sociology of Translation

name: John Law
description: British sociologist who developed heterogeneous engineering concept. Analyzed how technical and social elements are combined in building networks. Contributed to actor-network theory and science studies.

name: Trevor Pinch
description: British sociologist who developed social construction of technology (SCOT) with Bijker. Studied how interpretive flexibility and relevant social groups shape technology. Analyzed controversies in science.
key_works: The Social Construction of Technological Systems (co-editor), The Golem: What Everyone Should Know About Science

name: Wiebe Bijker
description: Dutch science and technology studies scholar who developed social construction of technology (SCOT) approach with Pinch. Analyzed technological frames and how different social groups shape technology.

name: Karen Barad
description: American physicist and feminist theorist who developed agential realism in 'Meeting the Universe Halfway' (2007). Challenged representationalism through quantum physics insights. Coined 'intra-action' replacing interaction to emphasize mutual constitution. Integrated feminism with new materialism and posthumanism.

name: New Materialisms
description: Philosophical approaches emphasizing matter's agency and vitality. Challenges anthropocentrism and representationalism. Draws on sciences, feminism, and post-humanism. Emphasizes intra-actions between human and non-human.

name: Jane Bennett
description: American political theorist who developed vital materialism in 'Vibrant Matter' (2010). Argued for thing-power and distributed agency across human and non-human. Applied new materialism to political ecology and ethics.

name: Posthumanism
description: Intellectual movement challenging human exceptionalism and nature/culture binary. Emphasizes distributed agency across human and non-human actors. Draws on science studies, feminism, and continental philosophy. Distinguishes from transhumanism.

name: Rosi Braidotti
description: Italian-Australian philosopher who developed nomadic theory and critical posthumanism in 'The Posthuman' (2013). Analyzes post-anthropocentric ethics and politics. Emphasizes affirmative ethics and zoe (life force).

name: Cary Wolfe
description: American posthumanist who theorized 'What is Posthumanism?' (2010). Distinguished posthumanism from humanism. Applied systems theory and deconstruction to animal studies and disability studies.

name: N. Katherine Hayles
description: American literary critic and posthuman theorist who wrote 'How We Became Posthuman' (1999). Analyzed cybernetics and information theory. Studied embodiment and posthuman subjectivity in literature and science.

name: Edward Said
description: Palestinian-American literary theorist who founded postcolonial studies with 'Orientalism' (1978). Analyzed how Western discourse constructed Orient as exotic Other, justifying colonialism. Applied Foucault's power/knowledge to imperialism. Influenced humanities profoundly.

name: Postcolonial Theory
description: Intellectual tradition analyzing colonialism's cultural, political, and economic legacies. Challenges Eurocentrism and recovers colonized voices. Examines how colonial discourse shaped knowledge. Key concepts include Orientalism, hybridity, and subaltern.

name: Subaltern Studies
description: Historiographical movement studying colonized peoples' perspectives. Founded by Ranajit Guha. Challenged elite nationalist histories. Applied Gramsci's subaltern concept to colonial India. Later integrated postcolonial theory and post-structuralism.

name: Ranajit Guha
description: Indian historian who founded Subaltern Studies Collective (1982). Wrote 'Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency' (1983) recovering peasant consciousness. Challenged both colonialist and nationalist historiography. Applied Gramscian concepts to colonial India.
key_works: Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India, Dominance without Hegemony

name: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
description: Indian-American literary theorist who wrote 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988), analyzing epistemic violence and subaltern's silence. Translated Derrida, bringing deconstruction to postcolonial studies. Developed strategic essentialism concept. Critiqued both Western feminism and nativism.
key_works: Can the Subaltern Speak?, A Critique of Postcolonial Reason

name: Dipesh Chakrabarty
description: Indian historian who wrote 'Provincializing Europe' (2000), challenging Europe as universal reference point. Later wrote 'Climate of History' essays (2009, 2014) analyzing Anthropocene's challenge to history. Integrated postcolonial theory with environmental history.
key_works: Provincializing Europe, The Climate of History in a Planetary Age

name: Partha Chatterjee
description: Indian political theorist and historian who wrote 'The Nation and Its Fragments' (1993), analyzing nationalism's contradictions in colonial context. Distinguished political and civil society. Contributed to subaltern studies.
key_works: The Nation and Its Fragments, The Politics of the Governed

name: Homi K. Bhabha
description: Indian-British postcolonial theorist who developed concepts of hybridity, third space, and mimicry in 'The Location of Culture' (1994). Analyzed ambivalence in colonial discourse. Applied psychoanalysis to postcolonialism.

name: Assemblage Theory
description: Ontological approach analyzing how heterogeneous elements combine into functional wholes while retaining autonomy. Developed from Deleuze and Guattari's assemblage concept. Applied to social theory, urbanism, and politics.

name: Manuel DeLanda
description: Mexican-American philosopher who developed realist interpretation of Deleuze in 'A New Philosophy of Society' (2006). Applied assemblage theory to social ontology. Emphasized emergence and non-linear causality.

name: Affect Theory
description: Interdisciplinary approach studying pre-cognitive bodily intensities and their political effects. Distinguishes affect from emotion. Draws on Spinoza, Deleuze, and neuroscience. Influential in cultural studies and queer theory.

name: Brian Massumi
description: Canadian political philosopher who developed affect theory in 'Parables for the Virtual' (2002). Analyzed relationship between affect, body, and politics. Draws on Deleuze and Spinoza.

name: Sara Ahmed
description: British-Australian feminist who wrote 'The Cultural Politics of Emotion' (2004) and 'Queer Phenomenology' (2006). Analyzed how emotions circulate and stick to bodies/objects. Developed queer phenomenology and willful subjects concept.
key_works: The Cultural Politics of Emotion, Queer Phenomenology, Living a Feminist Life

name: Lauren Berlant
description: American cultural theorist who developed concept of cruel optimism in 'Cruel Optimism' (2011). Analyzed affective attachments to fantasies that block flourishing. Studied intimate publics and slow death.

name: Stuart Hall
description: Jamaican-British cultural theorist who founded cultural studies through Birmingham School. Developed encoding/decoding model (1973) analyzing media reception. Theorized cultural identity as production, not essence. Integrated Marxism with post-structuralism.
key_works: Encoding and Decoding in the Television Discourse, Cultural Identity and Diaspora

name: Cultural Studies
description: Interdisciplinary field studying culture as site of power struggles. Analyzes popular culture, media, and identity. Founded at Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies. Integrates Marxism, feminism, and post-structuralism.

name: Richard Hoggart
description: British cultural studies founder who wrote 'The Uses of Literacy' (1957), analyzing working-class culture. Founded Birmingham Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (1964). Studied popular culture's relationship to power.

name: Raymond Williams
description: Welsh Marxist cultural theorist who developed cultural materialism. Wrote 'Culture and Society' (1958) and 'Keywords' (1976). Analyzed culture as whole way of life, not just art. Pioneered media studies and literary cultural analysis.
key_works: Culture and Society, Keywords, The Long Revolution

name: Global History
description: Historical approach studying processes transcending national boundaries. Emphasizes connections, circulations, and comparisons across regions. Challenges Eurocentrism through multi-sited research. Analyzes global networks and entanglements.

name: Sebastian Conrad
description: German global historian who wrote 'What is Global History?' (2016). Theorized global history's methods and challenges. Analyzed connections between imperialism and globalization.

name: Sanjay Subrahmanyam
description: Indian historian who developed connected histories approach. Studied early modern world through circulation and encounters. Challenged nation-centered histories through trans-regional analysis.

name: C.A. Bayly
description: British historian who wrote 'The Birth of the Modern World' (2004), synthesizing global history from 1780-1914. Analyzed multiple modernities and global connections. Integrated social, cultural, and political history globally.
key_works: The Birth of the Modern World

name: John McNeill
description: American environmental historian who wrote 'Something New Under the Sun' (2000), chronicling 20th-century environmental change. Pioneer in integrating environmental factors into historical analysis. Analyzed human-nature interactions at global scale.
key_works: Something New Under the Sun, Mosquito Empires

name: Environmental History
description: Historical approach analyzing human-environment interactions. Studies climate, disease, resources, and ecological systems. Challenges anthropocentrism by centering non-human nature. Addresses Anthropocene and planetary crises.

name: Anthropocene
description: Proposed geological epoch marked by human impact as dominant force shaping Earth systems. Challenges disciplinary boundaries and temporal scales. Debates starting date (industrial revolution, nuclear age, agriculture). Requires new historical thinking about species and planet.

name: Jason W. Moore
description: American environmental historian and world-ecologist who wrote 'Capitalism in the Web of Life' (2015). Developed world-ecology framework analyzing capitalism as way of organizing nature. Coined Capitalocene as alternative to Anthropocene.
key_works: Capitalism in the Web of Life

name: Anna Tsing
description: American anthropologist who wrote 'The Mushroom at the End of the World' (2015), analyzing matsutake mushrooms in capitalist ruins. Developed concepts of patchiness, assemblage, and contaminated diversity. Studies precarity and multispecies entanglements.
key_works: The Mushroom at the End of the World, Friction

name: Jo Guldi
description: American historian who co-wrote 'The History Manifesto' (2014) with Armitage, advocating for longue durée and policy engagement. Pioneered digital history methods including text mining and GIS.

name: Digital Humanities
description: Interdisciplinary field applying computational methods to humanities questions. Uses text mining, network analysis, GIS, and data visualization. Transforms archival research through digitization. Raises questions about algorithmic mediation and data epistemology.

name: Franco Moretti
description: Italian literary scholar who developed distant reading in 'Graphs, Maps, Trees' (2005). Applied quantitative methods to literary history. Analyzed form, genre, and literary evolution through computational methods.

name: Matthew Jockers
description: American digital humanist who applied computational methods to literary studies. Developed macroanalysis approach. Uses R programming for text mining and network analysis.

name: Lev Manovich
description: Russian-American digital culture theorist who wrote 'The Language of New Media' (2001). Analyzed digital media's properties and cultural logic. Pioneered cultural analytics using computational methods.
key_works: The Language of New Media, Software Takes Command

name: Linda Tuhiwai Smith
description: Māori scholar who wrote 'Decolonizing Methodologies' (1999), foundational for Indigenous research methodologies. Critiqued Western research as colonizing. Developed Indigenous research ethics emphasizing relationships, responsibility, respect, and reciprocity. Pioneered kaupapa Māori research.

name: Indigenous Methodologies
description: Research approaches grounded in Indigenous epistemologies and ethics. Emphasize relationality, ceremony, community accountability, and decolonization. Challenge Western research's extractive practices. Center Indigenous sovereignty over knowledge.

name: Shawn Wilson
description: Cree scholar who wrote 'Research is Ceremony' (2008). Developed relational accountability as Indigenous research paradigm. Argues research must strengthen relationships and serve community. Emphasizes Indigenous ontology and axiology.

name: Margaret Kovach
description: Plains Cree and Saulteaux scholar who wrote 'Indigenous Methodologies' (2009). Developed Indigenous inquiry grounded in tribal epistemologies. Analyzed story as method. Balances Indigenous and Western approaches pragmatically.

name: Rauna Kuokkanen
description: Sámi scholar analyzing Indigenous academia and research ethics. Critiques universities as colonial institutions. Advocates for Indigenous epistemic sovereignty and decolonizing knowledge production.

name: Critical Algorithm Studies
description: Interdisciplinary field analyzing algorithms' social, political, and ethical impacts. Studies bias in AI, platform governance, and automated decision-making. Emphasizes situated analysis of code and its effects.

name: Safiya Noble
description: American scholar who wrote 'Algorithms of Oppression' (2018), analyzing how search engines reinforce racism and sexism. Critiqued Google's bias. Pioneered critical algorithm studies and digital equity research.

name: Cathy O'Neil
description: American mathematician who wrote 'Weapons of Math Destruction' (2016), analyzing harmful algorithms in finance, education, and policing. Critiqued mathematical models' opacity and bias. Advocates algorithmic accountability.

name: Tarleton Gillespie
description: American media scholar analyzing platform politics. Wrote 'Custodians of the Internet' (2018) studying content moderation. Examines how platforms position themselves between publishers and neutral tools.
key_works: The Politics of 'Platforms', Custodians of the Internet

name: Platform Studies
description: Approach analyzing digital platforms' technical, economic, and social dimensions. Studies platform governance, APIs, and affordances. Examines how platforms shape culture and politics.

name: José van Dijck
description: Dutch media scholar who wrote 'The Culture of Connectivity' (2013), analyzing social media's transformation of sociality. Studies platform ecosystems and datafication. Analyzes platform society's implications.

name: Nick Srnicek
description: Canadian political economist who wrote 'Platform Capitalism' (2017), analyzing platforms as business model extracting and controlling data. Categorizes platform types and their economic logic.

name: Catherine D'Ignazio
description: American data scholar who co-wrote 'Data Feminism' (2020) with Klein. Applies intersectional feminism to data science. Advocates for data justice, situated knowledge, and challenging power in data systems.

name: Lauren Klein
description: American digital humanist who co-wrote 'Data Feminism' (2020) with D'Ignazio. Studies early American archives and visualization. Develops feminist approaches to computational methods and data representation.

name: Frantz Fanon
description: Martinique-born psychiatrist and anti-colonial theorist who wrote 'Black Skin, White Masks' (1952) analyzing colonialism's psychological effects, and 'The Wretched of the Earth' (1961) advocating decolonization through violence. Influenced postcolonial theory and black radical thought.
key_works: Black Skin, White Masks, The Wretched of the Earth

name: Achille Mbembe
description: Cameroonian historian and political theorist who developed necropolitics concept in 'On the Postcolony' (2001). Analyzes sovereignty as power over death. Studies African political thought and postcoloniality.

name: Walter Mignolo
description: Argentine semiotician who developed decolonial thinking. Analyzes coloniality of power, knowledge, and being. Advocates for epistemic disobedience and pluriversality. Part of modernity/coloniality research program.

name: Decolonial Theory
description: Latin American intellectual tradition analyzing coloniality persisting after formal colonization. Distinguishes coloniality from colonialism. Emphasizes epistemic violence and decolonization of knowledge. Advocates pluriversal thinking.

name: Aníbal Quijano
description: Peruvian sociologist who developed coloniality of power concept. Analyzed race as modern colonial invention organizing global capitalism. Founded modernity/coloniality research program.

name: Sigmund Freud
description: Austrian neurologist who founded psychoanalysis. Developed theories of unconscious mind, psychosexual development, and Oedipus complex in 'The Interpretation of Dreams' (1900) and later works. Introduced concepts of id, ego, superego, and defense mechanisms. Revolutionized understanding of mind and influenced humanities profoundly.
key_works: The Interpretation of Dreams, Civilization and Its Discontents, The Ego and the Id

name: Carl Jung
description: Swiss psychiatrist who developed analytical psychology, breaking from Freud. Introduced collective unconscious, archetypes, and individuation concepts. Studied mythology, religion, and symbolism. Influenced by eastern philosophy.

name: Jacques Lacan
description: French psychoanalyst who reinterpreted Freud through structural linguistics. Developed concepts of mirror stage, symbolic order, Real/Imaginary/Symbolic trinity, and objet petit a. Famous claim: 'the unconscious is structured like a language.'

name: Melanie Klein
description: Austrian-British psychoanalyst who developed object relations theory. Pioneered child psychoanalysis. Introduced concepts of paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions, projective identification.

name: Anna Freud
description: Austrian-British psychoanalyst and Sigmund Freud's daughter. Developed ego psychology emphasizing defense mechanisms. Pioneered child psychoanalysis and child development studies.
key_works: The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defense

name: Jean-Paul Sartre
description: French existentialist philosopher who wrote 'Being and Nothingness' (1943). Developed concepts of existence precedes essence, bad faith, and radical freedom. Combined phenomenology with existentialism. Engaged politically with Marxism.

name: Albert Camus
description: French-Algerian philosopher and author who developed absurdism in 'The Myth of Sisyphus' (1942). Analyzed tension between human need for meaning and meaningless universe. Advocated revolt and living without appeal.

name: Existentialism
description: Philosophical movement emphasizing individual existence, freedom, and choice. Argues existence precedes essence - humans define themselves through actions. Confronts anxiety, absurdity, and authenticity. Influenced by phenomenology and response to war.

name: Edmund Husserl
description: German philosopher who founded phenomenology in 'Logical Investigations' (1900-1901) and 'Ideas' (1913). Developed phenomenological reduction (epoché) bracketing assumptions to describe consciousness's structures. Emphasized intentionality - consciousness is always of something.

name: Martin Heidegger
description: German philosopher who wrote 'Being and Time' (1927), revolutionizing phenomenology through existential analysis. Analyzed Dasein (being-there) and temporality. Developed hermeneutic phenomenology. Later work focused on Being, technology, and language. Controversial due to Nazi involvement.
key_works: Being and Time, The Question Concerning Technology

name: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
description: French phenomenologist who wrote 'Phenomenology of Perception' (1945), emphasizing embodied experience. Challenged Cartesian mind-body dualism. Analyzed perception as primordial access to world. Influenced feminism and cognitive science.

name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
description: German philosopher who wrote 'Truth and Method' (1960), developing philosophical hermeneutics. Emphasized understanding as fusion of horizons between text and interpreter. Challenged objective interpretation. Analyzed tradition and prejudice positively.

name: Paul Ricoeur
description: French philosopher who integrated phenomenology, hermeneutics, and psychoanalysis. Wrote 'Time and Narrative' (1983-1985) analyzing narrative identity. Developed theory of metaphor and symbol.
key_works: Time and Narrative, The Symbolism of Evil

name: Discipline / Studies
description: Meta-category denoting academic areas of inquiry (e.g., history, sociology, anthropology, literary studies). Used to organize knowledge and practices across institutions.

name: Theoretical Framework
description: General explanatory structure guiding analysis and interpretation. Shapes questions, methods, and claims across disciplines.

name: Field / Sub-field / Sub-branch
description: Organizational levels within disciplines that define communities, journals, and debates (e.g., environmental history as a field within history).

name: Critical Perspective / Lens
description: Analytical stance foregrounding power, ideology, or identity (e.g., feminist, postcolonial, Marxist lenses) applied to interpret phenomena.

name: Theory
description: Systematic set of ideas explaining phenomena; often canonized and debated within fields. Provides concepts and propositions guiding research.

name: Conceptual Framework
description: Structured set of interrelated concepts used to map, explain, and investigate a problem space. Often operationalizes theories into research heuristics.

name: Methodology
description: Logic of inquiry linking theory and method; justifies why certain methods answer specific questions. Addresses validity, generalizability, and ethics.

name: Method
description: Practical techniques and procedures for gathering and analyzing evidence (e.g., discourse analysis, genealogy, ethnography).

name: Hegemony
description: Gramscian concept describing how ruling groups maintain dominance through cultural leadership and consent, not solely coercion. Central to cultural studies and postcolonial analysis.

name: Discourse Analysis
description: Analytical method studying how language and practices produce subjects, knowledge, and power relations. Applied across history, STS, and postcolonial studies.

name: Genealogy
description: Historical method (Nietzsche/Foucault) tracing contingent emergence of practices and concepts by analyzing discontinuities and power relations.

name: Actor-Network Theory
description: Approach in STS (Latour, Callon, Law) analyzing heterogeneous networks of human and non-human actants. Emphasizes symmetry and translation. Challenges social/technical divide.

name: Orientalism
description: Concept from Edward Said analyzing how Western discourse constructed the Orient as Other to justify empire; foundational to postcolonial theory.

name: Social Construction of Technology (SCOT)
description: Approach (Pinch & Bijker) showing technology development shaped by relevant social groups and interpretive flexibility; stabilization through closure.

name: Thomas S. Kuhn
description: American philosopher/historian of science who wrote 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' (1962). Introduced paradigms, normal science, and revolutionary change; argued science is not linear accumulation.
key_contributions: Paradigm shifts; normal vs. revolutionary science; incommensurability.
relevance_to_phd: Helps me frame how calibration regimes and measurement infrastructures might shift paradigms rather than simply evolve — i.e., the labour and recognition of technicians could play into paradigm-change rather than incremental addition.

name: Ludwik Fleck
description: Polish microbiologist and sociologist of knowledge; 'Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact' (1935). Developed thought styles and thought collectives shaping what counts as facts.
key_works: Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact
key_contributions: Thought styles & collectives; genesis of facts.
relevance_to_phd: Useful for thinking about epistemic communities engaged in sensor networks or satellite image interpretation: whose labour counts as 'fact' in climate data infrastructures, and whose is marginalised.

name: Sheila Jasanoff
description: American STS scholar of policy and governance. Developed concepts of co-production, civic epistemologies, and sociotechnical imaginaries.
key_works: Designs on Nature, The Fifth Branch
relevance_to_phd: Very strong fit: I can employ the co-production lens to explore how care ethics and labour-visibility in climate infrastructures are entangled with governance, measurement regimes, and imaginaries of the future.

name: Judy Wajcman
description: Feminist STS scholar analyzing gender, technology, and work; TechnoFeminism (2004) and related works.
key_contributions: Gender, technology and work; critique of symmetry.
relevance_to_phd: Directly relevant: I can use her feminist lens to look at the gendered (and other-axis) labour in calibration, sensor installation, monitoring, and how some of that labour is made invisible in climate-data infrastructures.

name: Annemarie Mol
description: Philosopher/STS scholar; 'The Body Multiple' (2002). Developed concepts of ontological politics and doing vs knowing; practice-oriented ontology.
relevance_to_phd: I can draw from her work to consider how technical infrastructures embody knowledge and labour; when multiple practices co-exist (e.g., farmer + remote-sensing technician) how is visibility of labour mediated?

name: Gabrielle Hecht
description: Historian of technology & environment; developed 'technopolitics'; work on nuclear infrastructures and environmental legacies.
key_works: The Radiance of France; Being Nuclear
relevance_to_phd: Especially relevant for environmental justice and measurement infrastructures: helps trace hidden labour in waste, monitoring, remediation infrastructures.

name: Shobita Parthasarathy
description: STS of innovation and comparative policy; governance of diagnostics and emerging technologies.
key_contributions: Comparative innovation governance; standards and diagnostics.
relevance_to_phd: Useful for my comparative angle: how different national/regional measurement infrastructures assign labour/visibility differently, and how I might map acknowledgement-transfer gaps.

name: Madeleine Akrich
description: Sociologist of technology; developed notion of artefact 'scripts' inscribing user roles and non-humans in technologies.
key_contributions: Scripts; design inscriptions; users as co-designers.
relevance_to_phd: Helps me ask: what script is inscribed into calibration sensors or satellite image pipelines, and how does that script render certain technicians’ labour visible/invisible?

name: Lucy Suchman
description: Anthropologist of human–machine interaction; 'Plans and Situated Actions' (1987). Developed situated action perspective.
relevance_to_phd: Focus on technicians and field agents interacting with remote-sensing systems: whose practices count, how visible are they, how are they recorded?

name: Ulrich Felt
description: STS scholar on changing role of science in society, participation, governance.
key_contributions: Public engagement; participation; governance of science.
relevance_to_phd: Frames how measurement labour involves engagement and participation; how 'care' might be recast as participation in monitoring infrastructures.

name: Wendy Faulkner
description: Feminist STS scholar on gender/technology, work, and power; critiques symmetry.
key_contributions: Gender, power and technology; critique of symmetry.
relevance_to_phd: Examine power inequalities within climate-monitoring infrastructures (who gets credit, who remains invisible) and link to labour and recognition gaps.

name: Co-production
description: Idea that science/technology and social order are co-produced (Jasanoff).

name: Sociotechnical Imaginaries
description: Collectively held visions of desirable futures realized through science/technology and institutions (Jasanoff & Kim).

name: Technopolitics
description: The strategic practice where technological choices and political dynamics co-constitute each other (Hecht).

name: Script
description: The notion that artefacts inscribe programs of action that configure users and non-humans (Akrich).

name: Situated Action
description: Perspective emphasizing action as situated in context rather than planned, shaping human–machine interaction (Suchman).

name: Ontological Politics
description: Politics of enacting different realities through practices; plural ontologies (Mol).

name: Sociology of Work, Labour, Organisations
description: Examines labour processes, organisations, hierarchical relations, and invisibility of labour (e.g., 'invisible work' in healthcare).
key_contributions: I can draw on this field to unpack how technicians, calibration engineers, sensor maintainers in climate/monitoring infrastructures perform labour that is often invisible or under-acknowledged; it gives me tools to talk about recognition, articulation work, and organisational invisibility.
relevance_to_phd: labour;work;organisation

name: Ethics of Care / Care Studies
description: Moral theory around care, relationality, dependency; emphasizes making visible caring labour and re-centering care.
key_contributions: Since my dissertation is about care ethics / labour-visibility, this lens asks how infrastructures of measurement enact or neglect care; how the labour of caring (for sensors, calibration, data quality) gets recognised.
relevance_to_phd: care

name: Infrastructure Studies
description: Studies infrastructures (technical, socio-technical) as sites of governance, maintenance, visibility/invisibility, and politics.
key_contributions: Analyze climate measurement infrastructures (ground stations, sensor networks, satellite data chains): who maintains them, whose labour keeps them running, whose work is rendered invisible, how infrastructures embody labour and calibration standards.
relevance_to_phd: infrastructure

name: Feminist Science & Technology Studies
description: Intersections of gender (and race/class) with science, technology, labour, bodies, and knowledge production; focuses on power and whose work counts.
key_contributions: Ask how gender/race/class dynamics shape the labour of calibration, monitoring, and maintenance in climate infrastructures; which bodies are visible/invisible.
relevance_to_phd: gender

name: Anthropology of Technology / Cultural Anthropology
description: Ethnographic approaches to how people interact with technologies; embodied know-how; technologies in everyday life.
key_contributions: Access micro-practices, embodied labour, and tacit knowledge of technicians and agents operating measurement infrastructures in specific cultural/institutional contexts.
relevance_to_phd: body

name: Science & Technology Policy / Governance Studies
description: How S/T are governed; how policy shapes standards, infrastructures, and expertise; co-production of knowledge and society.
key_contributions: Situate measurement infrastructures in governance: calibration standards, labour structuring by policy, institutionalisation (e.g., Swedish/European contexts) and effects on recognition of labour.
relevance_to_phd: policy

name: Environmental Justice / Political Ecology
description: How environmental problems, infrastructures, and measurement regimes intersect with justice; distribution of burdens/benefits; power and knowledge.
key_contributions: Link measurement, labour, and recognition to justice: which communities host sensor networks, whose labour is required, whose voices are heard/marginalised; tie care/labour of monitoring and memory (e.g., waste, legacy sensors) into justice.
relevance_to_phd: environment

name: Sociology of Quantification
description: How numbers, metrics, and statistics are produced; social embedding of measurement regimes and standards.
key_contributions: Calibration, sensor networks, and measurement are about quantification. Helps think through how labour supports standards and how invisibility shapes what counts in climate data infrastructures.
relevance_to_phd: quantification;standards;technology

name: Labour Geography / Geography of Work
description: Spatial dimensions of labour; how infrastructures and work practices map onto places; visibility across distance.
key_contributions: Climate measurement infrastructures are distributed (ground stations, remote sensors, satellites); this frames spatial visibility of labour and recognition across distance.
relevance_to_phd: earth;space;labour

name: Organisational Studies / Management Studies
description: How organisations coordinate work; how hidden work is managed; how care is operationalised in organisations.
key_contributions: Analyze how organisations (agencies, labs, satellite centres, calibration facilities) structure and manage labour and formalise/transform care and monitoring work; how recognition is organised.
relevance_to_phd: organisation;management;labour

name: Intersectionality
description: Analytical framework for understanding how systems of power (race, gender, class, etc.) intersect to shape experience and inequality. Coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw; developed by Black feminist thought and feminist STS.
key_contributions: Intersections of race, gender, class, etc.; structural vs. political intersectionality.
relevance_to_phd: Central for mapping how recognition and invisibility of labour in climate-data infrastructures vary along intersecting axes (gender, race, class, region).

name: Critical Posthumanism
description: Stream within posthumanism emphasizing critique of human exceptionalism, ethics, and more-than-human entanglements across science, technology, media, and ecology.
key_contributions: Affirmative ethics; decentring the human; more-than-human relations.
relevance_to_phd: Helps me theorize care/labour distributed across human–nonhuman constellations in measurement infrastructures (sensors, satellites, organisms, environments).

name: Joanna Zylinska
description: Media theorist and artist engaging posthumanism, AI, and the Anthropocene; authored 'Minimal Ethics for the Anthropocene' (2014) and 'AI Art: Machine Visions and Warped Dreams' (2020).
key_works: Minimal Ethics for the Anthropocene; AI Art
key_contributions: Minimal ethics; posthuman media; AI aesthetics.
relevance_to_phd: Useful to frame ethical and aesthetic dimensions of AI-enabled sensing/visualization within climate-data infrastructures.

name: Stefan Herbrechter
description: Cultural theorist who co-edited 'Critical Posthumanism' reader; develops critical posthumanities across media, culture, and theory.
relevance_to_phd: Adds depth to posthumanism network relevant for theorizing infrastructures and media of observation.

name: Kate Crawford
description: Scholar of AI, infrastructure, labour, and environment; 'Atlas of AI' (2021) analyzes extractive supply chains of AI. Co-founded AI Now Institute.
key_contributions: AI's extractive infrastructures; resource, labour, and environmental costs.
relevance_to_phd: Directly relevant to climate/earth observation infrastructures: connects AI pipelines, resource extraction, and invisible labour.

name: María Puig de la Bellacasa
description: STS and feminist theorist; 'Matters of Care' (2017). Develops speculative ethics of care in more-than-human worlds; connects care, technoscience, and ecology.
key_contributions: Care as ethical-political practice in technoscience; more-than-human care.
relevance_to_phd: Provides a care lens for maintenance, calibration, and ecological entanglements of measurement infrastructures.

name: Paul N. Edwards
description: Historian/STS scholar of climate knowledge infrastructures; 'A Vast Machine' (2010) on models, data, and global warming politics.
relevance_to_phd: Core reference for climate-data infrastructures, their politics, and labour of integration/calibration.

name: Lisa Parks
description: Media scholar of satellite cultures and media infrastructures; 'Cultures in Orbit' (2005) and later works on media/infrastructure politics.
key_contributions: Satellite/media infrastructures; visibility politics; remote sensing.
relevance_to_phd: Connects satellite cultures and media infrastructures to questions of visibility, labour, and governance in observation systems.

name: History of Computing
description: Historical study of computing technologies, institutions, labour, and infrastructures; examines standards, platforms, and global networks.
key_contributions: Computing histories; platforms; standards and institutions.
relevance_to_phd: Frames computing and data infrastructures (including satellites and sensors) as historically evolving socio-technical systems.

name: Martin Campbell-Kelly
description: Historian of computing; co-author of 'Computer: A History of the Information Machine' (with Aspray, Ensmenger, Akera). Studies software industry and information infrastructures.
key_works: Computer: A History of the Information Machine
key_contributions: History of computing and information infrastructures.
relevance_to_phd: Gives historical grounding for data/measurement infrastructures and organisational labour.

name: Data Feminism
description: Framework applying intersectional feminism to data science and visualization; centers power, justice, and situated knowledge (D'Ignazio & Klein).
key_contributions: Data justice; power; situated knowledges; feminist visualization.
relevance_to_phd: Supports an intersectional and justice-oriented approach to climate/measurement data and labour recognition.

name: Ruha Benjamin
description: Sociologist of science and technology; 'Race After Technology' (2019). Analyzes how technologies encode inequity; advocates for abolitionist tools and data justice.
key_contributions: Race and technology; data justice; abolitionist tools.
relevance_to_phd: Helps ground an intersectional analysis of measurement infrastructures and labour recognition across race/class lines.

name: Meredith Whittaker
description: AI policy leader and researcher; co-founded AI Now; focuses on AI governance, labour, and platform power.
key_contributions: AI governance; labor and organizing; platform power.
relevance_to_phd: Links AI policy and organizational dynamics to how measurement/AI infrastructures are governed and whose labour is recognised.

name: Shoshana Zuboff
description: Scholar who theorized surveillance capitalism in 'The Age of Surveillance Capitalism' (2019) – analyzing data extraction, behavioral futures, and platform power.
relevance_to_phd: Illuminates extraction logics and visibility of labour/infrastructures in platform economies relevant to AI and data pipelines.

name: Julie E. Cohen
description: Legal scholar of information law and political economy; 'Between Truth and Power' (2019). Analyzes datafication, platform power, and governance.
relevance_to_phd: Provides governance/legal lenses for measurement and AI infrastructures; how rules structure labour and recognition.

name: Sarah T. Roberts
description: Scholar of commercial content moderation; 'Behind the Screen' (2019). Reveals hidden labour and health impacts of platform moderation.
key_contributions: Hidden labour; commercial content moderation; platform operations.
relevance_to_phd: Central to invisible labour analysis; parallels maintenance/moderation work in data/measurement infrastructures.

name: Rob Kitchin
description: Geographer of data/infrastructures; 'The Data Revolution' (2014); studies smart cities, data assemblages, and governance.
relevance_to_phd: Frames data infrastructures and governance; relevant to sensors, platforms, and quantification practices.

name: Atlas of AI
description: Book by Kate Crawford analyzing AI's extractive infrastructures of data, labor, and resources; critical study of AI industry.
key_contributions: Critical atlas of AI's infrastructures; extraction and costs.
relevance_to_phd: Connects AI pipelines and invisible labor/resource extraction to climate and observation infrastructures.

name: A Vast Machine
description: Book by Paul N. Edwards on climate data/model infrastructures and the politics of global warming; canonical in climate knowledge infrastructures.
relevance_to_phd: Directly supports analysis of climate-data infrastructures, integration, and calibration labor.

name: Cultures in Orbit
description: Book by Lisa Parks on satellite media cultures and infrastructures; visibility politics of remote sensing.
key_contributions: Satellite/media infrastructures; visibility politics; remote sensing.
relevance_to_phd: Frames satellite cultures and media infrastructures relevant to observation systems and labor visibility.

name: Data Feminism (book)
description: Book by Catherine D'Ignazio and Lauren F. Klein applying intersectional feminism to data science, visualization, and justice.
key_contributions: Data justice; situated knowledges; feminist visualization.
relevance_to_phd: Supports intersectional and justice-oriented analysis of measurement/data infrastructures and labor recognition.

name: Algorithms of Oppression
description: Book by Safiya Umoja Noble analyzing search engine bias and digital racism; foundational to critical algorithm studies.
relevance_to_phd: Shows how information infrastructures encode bias, relevant to visibility/invisibility in data pipelines.

name: Race After Technology
description: Book by Ruha Benjamin examining how technologies encode inequity and race; proposes abolitionist tools.
relevance_to_phd: Grounds intersectional critique of measurement/AI infrastructures and labor recognition across race/class lines.

name: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
description: Book by Shoshana Zuboff theorizing data extraction, behavioral futures, and platform power.
relevance_to_phd: Explains extraction logics shaping platform and AI infrastructures with labor and governance implications.

name: Behind the Screen
description: Book by Sarah T. Roberts on commercial content moderation; reveals hidden labor and health impacts.
relevance_to_phd: Parallels maintenance/moderation work with data/measurement infrastructures and labor visibility.

name: Paris Agreement
description: Global climate accord under UNFCCC with commitments to limit warming; shapes climate monitoring and reporting infrastructures.
key_contributions: International climate governance; monitoring and reporting.
relevance_to_phd: Context for climate-data infrastructures and labor involved in monitoring and reporting.

name: Landsat 1 Launch
description: Launch of Landsat 1, pioneering Earth observation satellite; foundation for remote sensing data infrastructures.
relevance_to_phd: Historical anchor for observation infrastructures and related labor/maintenance.

name: Project Maven Protests
description: Employee protests against use of AI for military targeting (Google Project Maven); catalyzed debates on AI ethics and labor.
relevance_to_phd: Connects AI governance and labor visibility/agency within infrastructure organizations.

name: Establishment of ESA
description: European Space Agency founded; consolidation of European space programs; key role in Copernicus and Earth observation.
key_contributions: Institutional infrastructure for European space and observation programs.
relevance_to_phd: Sets organizational context for satellite infrastructures and associated labor.

name: Sputnik 1 Launch
description: Launch of Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite; catalyzed global space programs and remote sensing infrastructures.
key_contributions: First artificial satellite; global impetus for space infrastructure.
relevance_to_phd: Anchors the origins of satellite-based observation and related labor/institutions.

name: TIROS-1 Launch
description: Launch of TIROS-1, first successful weather satellite; foundation for meteorological remote sensing.
relevance_to_phd: Establishes climate and weather monitoring infrastructures.

name: TCP/IP Day
description: ARPANET switches to TCP/IP; foundational protocol for the modern Internet.
relevance_to_phd: Enables global networking underpinning data movement and platforms.

name: World Wide Web Proposal
description: Tim Berners-Lee proposes the World Wide Web at CERN; hypertext for sharing documents over the Internet.
relevance_to_phd: Transforms knowledge/data infrastructures used in humanities and observation systems.

name: CCD Sensor Invention
description: Invention of the charge-coupled device (CCD) by Boyle and Smith; revolutionizes imaging sensors.
key_contributions: Enables digital imaging across satellites and cameras.
relevance_to_phd: Core to remote sensing, scientific imaging, and data pipelines.

name: Infrared Radiation Discovery
description: William Herschel discovers infrared radiation; groundwork for thermal sensing.
relevance_to_phd: Underpins remote thermal sensing technologies.

name: Daguerreotype Announced
description: Louis Daguerre announces the daguerreotype; practical photography begins.
relevance_to_phd: Historical anchor for imaging technologies and cultural techniques.

name: AWS EC2 Launch
description: Amazon launches EC2 and S3; popularizes elastic cloud computing and modern data center practices.
relevance_to_phd: Shapes data infrastructure backends for analytics and AI pipelines.

name: GDPR Enforcement
description: General Data Protection Regulation comes into force in the EU; reshapes data governance and compliance.
key_contributions: Data protection regime in the EU.
relevance_to_phd: Alters governance of data infrastructures and recognition/accountability.

name: Snowden Disclosures
description: Edward Snowden reveals NSA surveillance programs; exposes global surveillance infrastructures.
relevance_to_phd: Reframes debates on data infrastructures and governance.

name: ImageNet Dataset Release
description: Release of ImageNet dataset; large-scale labeled images for computer vision research.
relevance_to_phd: Drives deep learning advances relevant to sensing and classification.

name: AlexNet Breakthrough
description: AlexNet wins ImageNet with deep CNNs; sparks modern deep learning wave.
